questions.question: Which statement best characterizes the difference between greedy decoding and beam search for sequence generation?
questions.choice_A: Greedy decoding searches over multiple candidate continuations while beam search commits to the single most probable token at each step.
questions.choice_B: Greedy decoding commits to the single most probable token at each step, while beam search maintains several high-probability partial sequences to hedge against early mistakes.
questions.choice_C: Both greedy decoding and beam search sample tokens stochastically but with different temperatures.
questions.choice_D: Beam search is equivalent to nucleus sampling when the beam size equals the top-p mass.

questions.question: How does temperature affect stochastic decoding under a softmax policy?
questions.choice_A: Temperature rescales logits linearly, uniformly increasing all probabilities by the same offset.
questions.choice_B: Increasing temperature concentrates probability mass on the top-1 token, reducing entropy.
questions.choice_C: Decreasing temperature sharpens the distribution, making high-probability tokens more likely and lowering entropy; increasing it flattens the distribution and raises entropy.
questions.choice_D: Temperature only affects tokens whose probabilities are below a fixed threshold and leaves high-probability tokens unchanged.

questions.question: What is the key difference between top-k and nucleus (top-p) sampling?
questions.choice_A: Top-k sampling selects tokens with probability above a fixed threshold, while nucleus sampling selects the top k tokens by probability.
questions.choice_B: Top-k sampling is deterministic, while nucleus sampling is stochastic.
questions.choice_C: Nucleus sampling is equivalent to beam search when p is small.
questions.choice_D: Top-k fixes the candidate set size to k tokens, whereas nucleus sampling chooses the smallest set of tokens whose cumulative probability exceeds p, yielding a variable set size.

questions.question: Which issue is beam search particularly prone to if not corrected, especially in open-ended generation?
questions.choice_A: Length bias, where shorter sequences are overpreferred unless length normalization or penalties are used.
questions.choice_B: Underexploration due to random sampling from low-probability tokens.
questions.choice_C: Overestimation of entropy because of temperature scaling.
questions.choice_D: Guaranteed mode collapse to a single hypothesis regardless of beam size.

questions.question: In the context of exploration for reasoning tasks, why might one prefer stochastic decoding over greedy decoding even if the model is well-calibrated?
questions.choice_A: Greedy decoding always increases variance across runs, harming reproducibility.
questions.choice_B: Stochastic decoding can traverse alternative promising reasoning paths that are not the single most probable next token, improving the chance that at least one sample reaches a correct solution.
questions.choice_C: Stochastic decoding guarantees a higher likelihood score for the final sequence.
questions.choice_D: Greedy decoding is incompatible with programmatic evaluation through unit tests.

questions.question: Which statement about tree search and structured exploration is most accurate?
questions.choice_A: Tree search is equivalent to sampling with temperature set to zero.
questions.choice_B: Tree search methods cannot incorporate learned value or policy guidance and must rely on uniform expansion.
questions.choice_C: Tree search (e.g., MCTS with UCT) can guide exploration toward promising branches using value estimates and visitation statistics, balancing exploration and exploitation.
questions.choice_D: Tree search is only applicable to tasks with deterministic transitions and fails with stochastic models.

questions.question: What is speculative decoding designed to achieve in autoregressive generation?
questions.choice_A: To increase diversity by randomly rejecting high-probability tokens.
questions.choice_B: To produce a different model distribution than the target model, trading accuracy for speed.
questions.choice_C: To prune low-probability beams more aggressively than standard beam search.
questions.choice_D: To accelerate sampling by using a fast draft model to propose tokens that are then verified or corrected by the target model, preserving the target model’s distribution.

questions.question: Which factor most directly governs the speedup obtained by speculative decoding?
questions.choice_A: The acceptance rate of proposed tokens from the draft model by the target model, which depends on the closeness of their conditional distributions.
questions.choice_B: The size of the vocabulary, independent of proposal quality.
questions.choice_C: The beam size used during verification.
questions.choice_D: The number of heads in the transformer’s attention layers.

questions.question: How do sampling budgets typically affect Pass@K when evaluating code generation with unit tests?
questions.choice_A: Pass@K is invariant to K and only depends on the best single sample.
questions.choice_B: Increasing K usually raises Pass@K because it increases the chance that at least one sample passes all tests, assuming independent errors across samples.
questions.choice_C: Pass@K decreases with larger K because more incorrect samples dilute the majority.
questions.choice_D: Pass@K is only defined for deterministic decoders like greedy decoding.

questions.question: Why can increasing diversity hurt Maj@K even when it helps Pass@K?
questions.choice_A: Maj@K and Pass@K are identical metrics and cannot move in opposite directions.
questions.choice_B: Maj@K is maximized when samples are as uncorrelated as possible.
questions.choice_C: Maj@K requires a majority of samples to agree on the correct answer; higher diversity can spread votes across multiple variants, reducing majority even if at least one is correct.
questions.choice_D: Pass@K penalizes diversity while Maj@K rewards it by design.

questions.question: In program-aided evaluation, why is it beneficial to execute candidate programs in a sandbox with unit tests?
questions.choice_A: It guarantees that the highest-log-probability program is always selected.
questions.choice_B: It replaces the need for any decoding strategy by deterministically computing the correct output.
questions.choice_C: It transforms open-ended evaluation into a grounded signal (pass/fail per test), allowing objective comparison of samples and enabling search strategies to be guided by execution feedback.
questions.choice_D: It removes the need to control for nondeterminism or flaky tests.

questions.question: Which practical consideration is most important when using unit-test-based evaluation for sampling?
questions.choice_A: Ensuring tests are robust and non-flaky, with proper isolation and time/resource limits to avoid false positives or negatives in measured Pass@K.
questions.choice_B: Always using greedy decoding to avoid divergent outputs.
questions.choice_C: Avoiding any sandboxing because it slows down evaluation.
questions.choice_D: Ignoring security and resource constraints to maximize coverage.

questions.question: What is a common failure mode of naive beam search in tasks requiring creativity or multi-solution diversity?
questions.choice_A: It increases entropy too aggressively, making outputs random.
questions.choice_B: Mode collapse across beams, where beams become near-duplicates due to local token-level scoring, reducing global diversity.
questions.choice_C: It underestimates the probability of the top-1 token.
questions.choice_D: It cannot be applied to sequences longer than 128 tokens.

questions.question: Which modification can mitigate length bias in beam search for open-ended generation?
questions.choice_A: Reducing vocabulary size at inference time.
questions.choice_B: Using top-k sampling with a small k.
questions.choice_C: Applying length normalization or a length penalty to the cumulative log-probability when ranking beams.
questions.choice_D: Increasing temperature beyond 1.5.

questions.question: How does nucleus sampling (top-p) typically affect the tail of the distribution compared to top-k sampling?
questions.choice_A: It always includes more tokens than any fixed k, increasing randomness.
questions.choice_B: It deterministically includes the same number of tokens per step, making it more stable.
questions.choice_C: It adapts the candidate set size to local uncertainty, allowing more tokens when the distribution is flat and fewer when it is peaked.
questions.choice_D: It eliminates the need for temperature scaling in all cases.

questions.question: Which of the following best captures the tradeoff between quality and diversity when choosing decoding parameters?
questions.choice_A: Lower temperature and smaller candidate sets (small k or p) typically increase local optimality and coherence but may miss alternative valid solutions; higher temperature and larger sets increase exploration but risk lower average quality per sample.
questions.choice_B: Higher temperature increases both quality and diversity monotonically.
questions.choice_C: Beam search strictly dominates stochastic methods in both quality and diversity.
questions.choice_D: Decoding parameters have negligible effect compared to training, so the tradeoff is irrelevant.

questions.question: In the context of accelerated sampling, which technique helps amortize computation across multiple samples sharing a prefix?
questions.choice_A: KV-cache reuse and tree-based batching, where previously computed key/value states for a prefix are reused to expand multiple continuations efficiently.
questions.choice_B: Increasing vocabulary size to reduce softmax cost.
questions.choice_C: Dropping normalization from the softmax to speed up sampling without affecting probabilities.
questions.choice_D: Using only CPU inference to avoid GPU memory constraints.

questions.question: What practical effect does increasing the sampling budget K have on evaluation under fixed compute constraints?
questions.choice_A: It always improves both Pass@K and latency.
questions.choice_B: It can improve Pass@K or Maj@K up to a point, but consumes more compute and latency; there are diminishing returns and potential opportunity costs (e.g., fewer prompts evaluated).
questions.choice_C: It has no effect on Pass@K as long as temperature is fixed.
questions.choice_D: It reduces diversity because samples become correlated.

questions.question: Which statement about speculative decoding’s correctness is true under the standard acceptance-rejection scheme?
questions.choice_A: It introduces a small bias that vanishes as the draft model improves.
questions.choice_B: If implemented correctly, it yields samples exactly distributed according to the target model, despite using a draft model to propose.
questions.choice_C: It matches the draft model’s distribution, not the target’s.
questions.choice_D: It only preserves correctness when the draft and target models are identical.

questions.question: How can program execution be used to guide structured exploration beyond passive evaluation?
questions.choice_A: By pruning any branch that fails a unit test and prioritizing branches that partially pass, one can use test outcomes as a heuristic to drive a search algorithm (e.g., MCTS or beam search with constraints).
questions.choice_B: By ignoring test outcomes to avoid overfitting to the test suite.
questions.choice_C: By always selecting the first program that compiles, regardless of correctness.
questions.choice_D: By replacing decoding entirely with a static analyzer.

questions.question: When comparing top-k and top-p at the same effective candidate set size on average, which configuration typically yields more stable quality across prompts?
questions.choice_A: Top-k, because it avoids pathological inclusion of many low-probability tail tokens in flat distributions and maintains a consistent exploration budget per step.
questions.choice_B: Top-p, because it enforces a fixed probability mass and thus a fixed number of candidates.
questions.choice_C: They are identical under any distribution.
questions.choice_D: Neither affects stability; only temperature matters.
